summary.text: In March 2026, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said AI adoption leadership is a crucial component of economic security and that Treasury is optimizing regulation to support growth while preserving national security. In June 2026, he said countries that deploy AI most effectively will shape the next era of growth and that Treasury will work with the financial sector to enable responsible AI adoption. Bessent has also said he supports open-source AI while warning that "open source is not open season on American IP," and he has linked AI to capex growth and infrastructure capacity constraints.

kids_chatbots.why: No statement addresses limits on AI chatbots for minors.

deepfakes.why: No statement addresses penalties for deepfakes or likeness rights.

election_ads.why: No statement addresses AI in election ads or political robocalls.

labeling.why: No statement addresses watermarking or AI disclosure mandates.

dc_moratorium.why: Bessent promotes AI infrastructure investment (s28, s35) but never explicitly rejects a data center moratorium; s7 reports unions' pushback, not his own position.

dc_ratepayers.why: s8 calls rising power costs a 'binding constraint' and urges building capacity, but says nothing about who should pay or about ratepayer cost allocation.

layoff_reporting.why: No statement addresses reporting or notice of AI-caused layoffs; s12 and s23 mention job growth generally.

bias_audits.why: No statement addresses bias testing or audits of AI decisions.

training_consent.why: s6 and s14 object to PRC firms misappropriating American IP, but do not address consent or payment for copyrighted training data.

preemption.why: No statement addresses a federal standard overriding state AI laws.

chips.why: s10 supports outbound investment screening and s24 criticizes China's export controls, but neither addresses stricter U.S. AI chip export controls.

testing_mandate.why: s31 notes labs are 'working on safety' but does not call for mandatory pre-release testing or audits.

transparency.why: No statement calls for published safety plans, incident reports, or model information sharing.

whistleblowers.why: No statement addresses AI whistleblower protections.

liability.why: Bessent explicitly urged lawmakers not to give frontier labs the liability exemption they are seeking, supporting developer liability for AI harms.

misuse.why: s33 discusses using frontier AI for cybersecurity defense, not rules requiring safeguards against weapons-related misuse.

nuclear.why: No statement addresses human control of nuclear launch.

autonomous_weapons.why: No statement addresses human control of lethal force or autonomous weapons.

licensing.why: General deregulatory rhetoric (s1, s11, s26) does not name licensing or a new AI agency.

intl_agreement.why: s16 and s20-s22 concern trade, currency, and coordinated pressure on China, not an AI safety treaty or formal AI risk agreement.

pause.why: s34's competitive framing ('nothing else matters') does not explicitly reject a pause or slowdown on frontier AI.

rsi.why: No statement addresses limits on self-improving AI or automated AI research.

superintelligence.why: No statement addresses a ban on superintelligence.

statements.text: Economic security – the condition of having secure and resilient domestic production capacity – is core to financial stability, and leadership in AI adoption is a crucial component of economic security,” said U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “We are optimizing regulation to support growth for both Main Street and Wall Street: moving from a posture focused on constraint toward one that recognizes failure to adopt productivity-enhancing technology as its own risk.

statements.text: The proposed regulations would strengthen the existing Outbound Investment Security Program to prevent our adversaries from using U.S. investment to develop critical technologies that threaten U.S. national security. This important step also helps promote our commitment to an open investment environment by providing clarity to U.S. and foreign investors as well as an opportunity for them to provide feedback on the proposed regulations.

statements.text: We are optimizing regulation to support growth for both Main Street and Wall Street: moving from a posture focused on constraint toward one that recognizes failure to adopt productivity-enhancing technology as its own risk. The Treasury Department will continue evaluating regulatory frameworks and enforcement policies to enable the U.S. financial sector’s leadership in AI adoption while preserving national security and long-term economic resilience.
